claim: An American writer argued that women ought to have an education in her book from 1792. This writer was friends with Fanny Blood.
evidencia:
Page: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. Sentence: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: with Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects (1792), written by the 18th-century British proto-feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, is one of the earliest works of feminist philosophy.
Page: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. Sentence: She argues that women ought to have an education commensurate with their position in society, claiming that women are essential to the nation because they educate its children and because they could be "companions" to their husbands, rather than mere wives.
Page: Mary Wollstonecraft. Sentence: Mary Wollstonecraft ( ; 27 April 1759 – 10 September 1797) was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights.
Page: Fanny Blood. Sentence: Frances "Fanny" Blood (1758 - November 29, 1785) was an English illustrator and educator and longtime friend of Mary Wollstonecraft.

Facts:
- Frances "Fanny" Blood was born in 1758 and was an English illustrator and educator.
- Mary Wollstonecraft was born on 27 April 1759 and was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights.
- Frances "Fanny" Blood was a longtime friend of Mary Wollstonecraft.
- Frances "Fanny" Blood died on 29 November 1785.
- In 1792, Mary Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: with Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects.
- A Vindication of the Rights of Woman is one of the earliest works of feminist philosophy.
- In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women should receive an education suited to their position in society.
- In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women are essential to the nation because they educate children and can be companions to their husbands rather than mere wives.
- Mary Wollstonecraft died on 10 September 1797.
